Former Army Ranger sniper Nicholas Irving and former Navy SEAL Robert O’Neill join Vlad to break down global conflict, Iran peace talks, Donald Trump, midterm election strategy, gas prices, OPEC, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, the IRGC, the Red Sea, and the Strait of Hormuz. --------
T.K. Kirkland sits down with Vlad to clear up the viral video that had fans believing he was involved in a fight with Mike Epps. Kirkland says the clip was not real and that the people in the video only resembled them from certain angles, skin tone and profile. He explains that Mike personally called him about the rumors, and T.K. wanted to publicly set the record straight about their longtime friendship.

Kirkland reflects on knowing Mike Epps since the early 1990s, including meeting him in Atlanta, Georgia, bringing him to New York City, and staying close through decades in comedy. He calls Epps one of the greatest comedians and actors of their era and says there has never been serious conflict between them. The conversation also touches on Mike’s Indiana roots, his loyal crew, and why T.K. says their bond remains “family.”

--------
Max B sits down with VladTV to discuss his upbringing in Harlem, his rise in music, his relationships with Jim Jones and French Montana, and the legal case that ultimately cost him nearly 18 years of his life.
Max reflects on growing up in the Abraham Lincoln Houses and spending much of his childhood in the Hawthorne group home, where he says structure and organized activities helped shape him. He also opens up about losing his older brother Eric and how that tragedy affected him at a young age.
The conversation then turns to Max's music career, including signing with Jim Jones in the mid-2000s and contributing to Diary of a Summer. He discusses the development of his signature melodic style, his chemistry with French Montana, and how projects like Coke Wave helped build momentum for both artists. Max also talks about his versatility and the response to newer music following his release.
A major portion of the interview focuses on the robbery case involving Gina Conway and Pooh Sims. Max explains his role in the planning while maintaining that he was not present for the violence or murder that occurred. After initially receiving a 75-year sentence, he describes the post-conviction process that eventually led to a new plea agreement and a reduced 20-year sentence.
Max was released in 2025 after serving approximately 17 years and 10 months. He reflects on returning home, rebuilding his career, and preparing new projects including Wavy Pain, while adjusting to a music industry that changed dramatically during his incarceration.

--------
Trap Lore Ross returns to VladTV to discuss the death of Chicago rapper Bloodhound Q50 and break down the surprising outcome of Lil Durk's federal murder-for-hire trial.
Ross and Vlad first react to Q50 being killed at just 22 years old after he was shot inside a Tesla outside a Chicago gas station. They discuss his rise alongside the late Lil Jeff, his reputation for claiming involvement in multiple killings, and the numerous street conflicts surrounding his career. Vlad reflects on previously interviewing Q50 and warns young artists that success doesn't erase unresolved street problems.
The conversation then shifts to Lil Durk's trial, which Ross attended in person. Durk was found not guilty on five counts connected to the murder-for-hire case involving the death of Lil Pab, while co-defendants Dee Dee and David Lindsay were convicted of stalking resulting in death. Ross explains why he believes prosecutors presented significant circumstantial evidence but ultimately failed to eliminate reasonable doubt surrounding Durk's direct involvement.
They examine key evidence presented during the trial, including testimony from Vonnie, travel arrangements allegedly made for individuals involved in the shooting, and flights reportedly purchased using Durk's American Express card.
Despite the acquittal, Durk's legal problems may not be over. Ross and Vlad discuss severed charges and a potential future RICO case involving additional alleged murders and attempted murders, including the attempted killing of Quando Rondo. They also examine whether additional defendants could cooperate with federal prosecutors before future trials.
Finally, they discuss the possibility of a civil lawsuit from Lil Pab's mother, where the burden of proof would be lower than in the criminal case.

In this VladTV interview, Denvonta “Dirt Rocc” Lee revisits the infamous mall brawl involving Trayvon Lane, members of the Crips and Bloods, and the much-discussed Death Row chain. Dirt Rocc breaks down what happened outside Foot Locker before the fight spilled inside, explaining that the chain came off during the chaos but was not intentionally snatched or stolen by South Side Crips. He says Trayvon Lane’s long-standing claim that nobody took his chain is true.

Dirt Rocc also describes the scene as seven people fighting, with store damage leading to a Foot Locker remodel, while mall security struggled to intervene before the Lakewood Sheriff arrived. Despite the rumors surrounding Death Row Records, gang politics, and the confrontation, he says no one was seriously injured—just bumps, bruises, and a story that grew larger over time.

In this VladTV interview, political consultants Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl respond to CBS’ 60 Minutes report with Lesley Stahl, including the hidden-camera meeting involving convicted wildlife trafficker Amon Corvino and a proposed $300,000 Trump pardon effort. The pair defend their paid advocacy work and address claims surrounding Joseph Schwartz, a Jewish nursing home-chain owner convicted in a tax fraud case, saying they were paid about $968,000—near the reported $1 million fee—before Donald Trump granted him clemency. Wohl and Burkman argue the New Jersey case was mishandled, cite COVID-era nursing home scrutiny tied to Andrew Cuomo, and accuse the judge of anti-Semitic remarks. They also discuss the DOJ pardon process, Ed Martin, Article II presidential powers, and contrast Trump’s pardons with Joe Biden’s controversial clemency decisions involving Hunter Biden and Anthony Fauci. Martin Shkreli and DOJ charging tactics are also referenced.

The entertainer and RuPaul’s Drag Race judge discusses beginning her transition around 17, finding underground hormones in the mid-1990s, and later getting silicone injections before BBLs became mainstream. She also opens up about being fired from jobs at Publix, Long John Silver’s, and TracFone/Top Telecom while transitioning, eventually turning to sex work on 79th Street in Miami after feeling pushed out of traditional employment.
